title: One Ringgit for an Airline That Was 'About Dead'
dek: In 2001 a music executive with no airline experience took over a failing Malaysian carrier for a token ringgit and its debts, and mortgaged his house to run it.

story.event: Taking over a failing airline for one ringgit plus its debts
story.summary: In 2001 Tony Fernandes, who had just left Warner Music, set out to start a low-cost airline in Malaysia; told no new licences would be issued, he and Kamarudin Meranun took over the loss-making AirAsia from DRB-Hicom, with two ageing Boeing 737s and about RM40 million of debt, for a token one ringgit. Fernandes mortgaged his house for working capital, and AirAsia relaunched as a no-frills carrier in January 2002, carrying about a million passengers in its first year.
paragraphs: In 2001 Tony Fernandes, a 37-year-old Malaysian who had run Warner Music's South-East Asian business, left the company, cashing in about $250,000 of stock options, and flew home from New York by way of London. In Britain he saw easyJet's founder, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, on television explaining no-frills flying. He took a train to the airline's base at Luton, spent a day talking to its passengers and staff, then rang his wife to say he was going to start an airline. "She thought I was a lunatic," he later said.

He had no airline experience. A former Ryanair executive, Conor McCarthy, told him to drop his dream of long-haul flights and start short-haul. By Fernandes's later account, a newspaper statistic that only six per cent of Malaysians had ever flown persuaded him there was a market. With friends from the music business, he sought a meeting with the prime minister, Mahathir Mohamad, to ask for a licence. No new licences would be issued, Fernandes recalled being told, but they could take over a struggling carrier. "One airline was beyond hope while the other was about dead. We chose the one that was about dead."

That was AirAsia, a loss-making subsidiary of the state-linked conglomerate DRB-Hicom, with two ageing Boeing 737s, about 200 staff and some RM40 million of debt. Fernandes and his partner Kamarudin Meranun took it over through their company, Tune Air, for a token one ringgit plus the debt, and Fernandes mortgaged his house for working capital. Air travel was in a slump after the attacks of 11 September; accounts differ on whether the terms were agreed just before them or just after.

AirAsia relaunched as a no-frills carrier in January 2002, advertising fares from nine ringgit. Before the first flight, he recalled, "I realised we had no food," so he took the crew to a supermarket for drinks and sandwiches. By the end of its first year the airline had carried about a million passengers, and by mid-2003 it was making a profit. Analysts had been sceptical. "They said we would die," Fernandes told Businessweek in 2004.

quote.text: Let our undertakings, therefore, be neither petty nor yet presumptuous and reckless: let our hopes not range far from home: let us attempt nothing which if we succeed will make us astonished at our success.
quote.work: Of Anger, addressed to Novatus (Minor Dialogues)
quote.source_title: Minor Dialogues, Together With the Dialogue on Clemency, tr. Aubrey Stewart, Project Gutenberg eBook #64576
quote.connection: Seneca would have counselled against almost everything here: no experience, a mortgaged house, a carrier its new owner called about dead, bought in an aviation slump. AirAsia's success does not show that he was wrong, only that this time the undertaking held.

reflection: This story is usually told as proof that bold bets pay. Seneca would tell it another way: a man took on a burden far beyond his experience, put his family's house under it, and happened to carry it. Both readings can be true at once.

If you are weighing a larger step for talQen, it may help to separate two questions that blur together when you are tired: whether the idea is good, and whether the people who would share the cost of failure have agreed to share it. When Fernandes made up his mind, he said, he rang his wife.
invitation: Before your next large commitment, write one sentence on what failure would cost the people at home. Today, just write the sentence; deciding whether to show it to them can wait.

research_notes: Debt figures disagree. RM40 million is given by Key.Aero (2024), AFP via The Daily Star (2014) and Wikipedia; Bloomberg Businessweek (2004) and the 2014 Sunday Times column give US$11 million, which matches RM40 million at the 2001 peg of about RM3.80 to the dollar; MoneyWeek (2009) says 'pounds 5m'; Forbes Asia (2010) says '$40 million', which appears to confuse ringgit with dollars; a 2018 Star article (not accessible to the checker) mentions RM190 million in liabilities, probably a wider measure. The story uses 'some RM40 million of debt'. Dates disagree too: Wikipedia (citing an AirAsia newsroom page) dates the acquisition to 5 September 2001, other accounts to 8 September, days before the 11 September attacks; Bloomberg (2004) dates Fernandes's meeting with Mahathir to October 2001, and AFP says he took over 'shortly after' the attacks; Wikipedia's Tune Group page gives 2 December 2001 for the purchase; the Sunday Times column even says 2002. The story says only that accounts differ on whether terms were agreed before or after the attacks. First flight: 8 January 2002 (MoneyWeek) versus a relaunch on 15 January 2002 (Wikipedia); the story says January 2002. The six-per-cent statistic, the Mahathir meeting and the 'about dead' quotation come from Fernandes's own keynote account as retold by a Sunday Times columnist, so they are attributed to his later account; Mahathir's reported words are paraphrased, not quoted. Partners: Key.Aero and the New Straits Times name Kamarudin Meranun; some accounts add Aziz Bakar, Pahamin Rajab and Conor McCarthy as partners, while MoneyWeek presents McCarthy as an adviser; the story names Kamarudin as partner and McCarthy as giving advice. Staff: 'about 200' is from Key.Aero only. Outcomes: the million passengers in the first year and profit by June 2003 are from MoneyWeek, with Forbes saying he 'quickly' made it profitable; claims elsewhere that all debts were cleared within one or two years differ and are not used. Funding is 'mixed': the founders' own money (stock options, a mortgaged house) and partners, with the airline's existing debt assumed. The company is written 'AirAsia (later Capital A)' because the listed group, formerly AirAsia Group, was later renamed Capital A (Key.Aero) while the airline kept the AirAsia name. The Sunday Times PDF loads but its text is not machine-read by the checker. The Seneca passage is from his advice on avoiding anger by not overreaching, applied here by analogy.
